# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.

Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.

- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. Three findings worth having before you decide:

1. **This repo has exactly one open tracker: [#904](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/904) `[claudinite] CI performance`.** It was created 2026-08-16, *before* [#951](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/951) taught `createTracker` to close on create — and nothing in the library ever repairs a tracker that is already open. `findOrCreateTracker` returns it as-is, forever.
2. **`[claudinite] CI performance` is off-convention twice over.** It doesn't carry the `Claudinite tracker:` prefix, so it isn't matched by the signals filter in `engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs:180` — meaning it's already visible to `tidy-issues` as ordinary project work.
3. **Trackers are deliberately hidden from `tidy-issues`.** That filter exists because a tracker rewrite lands in `issues.touched` and would wake `tidy-issues` on the queue's own churn (F8). So "tidy-issues closes open trackers" means either unhiding them (re-opening F8) or giving `tidy-issues` a second, separate sweep over hidden titles.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.

Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

content.text:
Answering your ci-performance question first, then the inventory.

**`ci-performance` (basics pack) — what its tracker is.** It's the only tracker that isn't a log: it's the *measurement itself*. The weekly code-work reads `actions/runs`, takes each workflow's median over the last 7 days against the 7 before, and rewrites the tracker body with that table plus the slowest steps of the slowest workflow's latest run — [`worker.mjs:169-176`](packs/basics/tasks/ci-performance/worker.mjs). A quiet week ends there, no agent spent. Only a real regression (≥1.25x **and** ≥20s, ≥3 runs each window) adds a dated comment and hands the issue number to the agentic phase as `delivered.issue`, which is how the agent knows where to report. In this repo that's [#904](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/904) — and it's **open**, which is the one bug I found: `createTracker` creates-then-closes in two calls and returns `leftOpen`, but the worker destructures only `number` and drops it, and nothing ever re-closes a tracker found open. So #904 has sat open since 2026-08-16, and its title doesn't match the `^claudinite tracker:` filter in [`signals/index.mjs:180`](engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs), so tidy-issues sees it as ordinary project work.

**The 11 tasks that create a tracker:**

| Task | Pack | Title | How |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ci-performance` | basics | `[claudinite] CI performance` | code-work |
| `growth-dedup` | claudinite-growth | `Claudinite tracker: Growth Dedup` | code-work |
| `growth-extract` | claudinite-growth | `Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract` | agentic |
| `growth-discover-packs` | claudinite-growth | `Claudinite tracker: Discover Local Packs` | agentic |
| `prose-to-checks-sweep` | claudinite-growth | `Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks` | agentic |
| `rule-revalidation` | claudinite-growth | `Claudinite tracker: Rule Revalidation` | agentic |
| `jwt-advisory-watch` | jwt | `Claudinite tracker: JWT advisory watch` | agentic |
| `wiki-growth` | product-wiki | `Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth` | agentic |
| `tidy-issues` | tidy-repo | `Claudinite tracker: Tidy Issues` | agentic |
| `tidy-prs` | tidy-repo | `Claudinite tracker: Tidy PRs` | agentic |
| `tidy-branches` | tidy-repo | `Claudinite tracker: Tidy Branches` | agentic |

Two of them consume their tracker rather than just writing it, so dropping it needs a replacement, not just a deletion:

- **`rule-revalidation`** slices its next run from its own log — "the claims longest since their last recorded probe, per the tracker's log". No log, no slice.
- **`growth-dedup`** puts its brief *on* the tracker and passes only the number to the agentic phase; that's a deliberate design so the agent can't read a stale copy.

Both fit your `VERSIONS.md` idea if the file carries enough — a dated line per rule added/removed and per check created gives `growth-dedup` its brief source, but `rule-revalidation` needs a *probe date per claim*, which is a different record.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

# Rule revalidation — re-probe the claims whose truth lives outside this repo

Most of a pack's prose is judgment: how to approach a change, what to do first, what never to do. Judgment does not expire. A smaller set of rules is different — each one asserts a **fact about the environment**: that the harness accepts a call in a certain shape, that the Action's token can or cannot reach a path, that an MCP tool exists, that a platform behaves a particular way. Those were true on the day they were written and are true today only by luck, because nothing in this repo turns red when a platform moves under them. The prose stays green, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost arrives as a session spent on a route that closed.

This task re-runs the probe behind each such claim, weekly, and corrects what no longer holds.

The run's **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to revalidate and the two probe rules below. Work those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. A canon pack a repo only mounts is revalidated in the repo that owns it, on this same task.

Open a PR and leave it for review. This task rewrites the rules sessions obey, on evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive from the diff, so every run's changes go in front of the owner.

## What counts as a revalidatable claim

A sentence in a rule, a check's `failureMessage` or `fix` text, or a skill's procedure, that would be **falsified by a change nobody in this repo makes**. The three richest seams:

- **The Claude environment** — tool contracts and their failure modes (what `Edit` requires before it will apply, what a scheduling call rejects, what a search returns for a bare name), which harness surfaces exist, what a session can and cannot see.
- **GitHub permissions and API behaviour** — what the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may push or label, what a path refuses, which status a call returns, what a repository setting gates.
- **MCP functions** — that a named tool exists, what its parameters are called, what it returns, which server carries it.

Also fair game: any rule naming a version floor, a runtime's behaviour, or an external service's response shape.

**Not** in scope, and left alone without a probe: judgment and taste rules; rules about how *this* repo is organized (a check already guards those, and a stale one fails loudly); product requirements; anything whose truth a reviewer could settle by reading the tree.

## The probe

A claim is revalidated by **executing the smallest thing that would distinguish true from false**, and reporting what actually happened — never by recalling what you know, and never by reasoning from the rule's own wording.

Two rules bound it, both binding scope from the dispatch:

1. **Read-only.** Probe by doing the harmless half: call the tool and read its schema, request the resource, run the command that reports rather than acts. A claim whose probe would **write, delete, merge, publish, notify, or spend a credential** is not probed — verify it against authoritative documentation and say in the log that documentation, not a run, is the evidence.
2. **A probe you cannot run is `unprobed`, not disproven.** This session carries the reach its repo was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under. A tool that is absent *here*, a permission denied *to this session*, a network path the sandbox blocks — none of that is evidence the claim is stale. Leave the rule exactly as it stands, log it as unprobed, and move on. Rewriting a rule into "you cannot do X" because *this* session could not is the single worst outcome available to this task: it is unfalsifiable afterwards, and it removes a capability from every future session.

## What a run does

1. **Slice.** The corpus is standing and mostly stable, so a run takes a **slice**, not the whole thing: the claims longest since their last recorded probe, per the tracker's log, plus any the log has never covered. Prefer the claims whose staleness would cost most — a rule that would send a session down a dead path beats a version number in a comment. Ten well-probed claims beat forty skimmed.
2. **Probe each**, per the rules above, and record what you ran and what came back.
3. **Correct what is stale**, as far as the probe reaches and no further — one probe answers one claim, and a neighbouring claim it seems to imply gets its own probe. Rewrite the rule to what the probe showed, in the same voice and at the same length, and carry the *new* fact — not a note about the correction, and not a dated changelog. Where the claim was a check's premise rather than prose, and the check itself is now asserting a dead fact, fix the check and its fixture. Where a claim has become simply irrelevant (the surface it describes is gone), delete the rule whole rather than trimming it toward nothing.
4. **Open a PR** — one per run, on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. The PR body is the evidence a reviewer cannot re-derive: per changed rule, the probe run and its result. Keep the repo's offline test suite green.
5. **Log to the tracker.** The standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Rule Revalidation`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing — creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument, so create it and close it in a second call. **Never open, close, or reopen it** afterward. Log each run as a dated comment listing every claim probed with its verdict — `holds`, `stale (corrected)`, `unprobed (why)`, or `doc-verified` — because that list is what the *next* run slices against. A run that found everything still true logs exactly that.

> a run takes a **slice**, not the whole thing: the claims longest since their last recorded probe, **per the tracker's log**, plus any the log has never covered.

So the tracker isn't a record there — it's *state*. Each run's dated comment lists every claim probed with its verdict, and the next run reads that list to pick the ten it hasn't touched in longest. Drop the tracker and the task has no memory of what it already probed.

Your framing removes the need for it: a weekly task that probes **every** environment-fact claim in the pack has nothing to remember. | `tidy-branches` | keep | untouched — #1240 removes the task |
| `ci-performance` | `[claudinite] CI performance` | keep — it is a live measurement table, not a growth log |

## The record that replaces them

`VERSIONS.md` at the root of each local pack (`.claudinite/local/packs/<id>/VERSIONS.md`): every addition or removal of a prose rule, and every check created, by whichever automatic task did it. One dated line per change, newest first. It is in the pack, so it travels with the pack, diffs in a PR, and survives an issue sweep.

## Two engine fixes that come with it

- `findTracker`/`findOrCreateTracker` re-close any tracker they find **open**. `createTracker` has closed on create since #951, but nothing ever repaired a tracker created before that — which is why #904 has sat open since 2026-08-16.
- `[claudinite] CI performance` is added to the hidden-titles filter in `engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs`. It is off-convention, so `tidy-issues` currently sees it as ordinary project work.

## Why `growth-dedup` cannot simply drop its issue

Its tracker is not a log — it is the carrier for the window brief, because there is no code→agent data channel (`worker.mjs:16`). Code-work already receives `CLAUDINITE_ITEM`, the work item's own issue number, so the brief becomes a comment there: per-run, which is what the brief already is, and it dies with the item.

## Why `rule-revalidation` loses its slicing

`task.md:34` picks the ten claims longest since their last recorded probe **per the tracker's log**. The tracker is state, not a record. A weekly run that probes every environment-fact claim needs no memory, and the judgment prose is already out of scope — so the set is far smaller than the corpus.

content.content:
## Rules expire when the environment moves — revalidation

Capture, dedup and conversion all assume a rule is either right or superseded. A third failure mode
has no local signal at all: the rule was right, and the **world** changed. A claim that the harness
rejects a call in some shape, that the Action's token cannot push a path, that an MCP tool exists —
each is a fact about a platform this repo does not control, and when it stops being true nothing
here goes red. The prose keeps reading as authoritative, sessions keep obeying it, and the cost
lands as a session spent on a route that closed.

[rule-revalidation](tasks/rule-revalidation/task.md) is the weekly re-probe. It slices the corpus by
longest-since-probed, **runs** the smallest read-only thing that would distinguish true from false
for each environment-dependent claim, and corrects what the probe contradicts — in a reviewed PR
whose body carries the probe evidence, since that is the one thing a reviewer cannot re-derive from
the diff. Its scope is the same `pack_paths` config `prose-to-checks-sweep` reads, so a repo names
its capture surface once.

The dangerous verdict is the one it refuses to reach. An executor session carries the reach its
repo's routine was provisioned with, which is not the reach every rule was written under, so a probe
that cannot run is logged **unprobed** and the rule is left untouched. Rewriting a rule into "you
cannot do X" because one session could not is unfalsifiable afterwards and removes the capability
from every future session — which is why the corpus each run touches is small and every verdict is
logged on a standing tracker, including the ones that changed nothing.

## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)

Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
project's own content;
the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).

Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** whose failure message carries the lesson —
a **declared** one in the owning pack's `declared-checks.json` wherever patterns over files can say it,
a **rule module** in its `rules` only where they can't — an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack
skill**, and only what none of those can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.

The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.

that cannot run is logged **unprobed** and the rule is left untouched. Rewriting a rule into "you

from every future session — which is why the corpus each run touches is small and every verdict is
logged on a standing tracker, including the ones that changed nothing.

## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)

Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
project's own content;
the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray

project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).

project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** whose failure message carries the lesson —

context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.

The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).

A routine whose output lands **in the repo** already has a record: the commit, the PR and the file it changed, which diff, carry history, and sit where a reader is already looking, none of which an in-place-rewritten issue body does. Where a tracker does earn its place, title it exactly `Claudinite tracker: <Name>`. Find it by that **exact title string, never a fuzzy or partial match** and never a bare number (a number can dangle, and a partial match risks landing on the wrong issue). Log every run that produces a change there — as a **dated comment**, not a sub-issue — so the routine's output accumulates in one reviewable feed, making it easy to audit what it did over time and to tell when the routine itself needs tuning. One issue per routine, not a shared parent. **Create it already closed** if it doesn't exist yet — that is **two calls**, because issue creation always lands the issue open and a `state: closed` argument on the create call is silently ignored: create it, then close it with a follow-up update. And **never open, close, or reopen it again afterward** — its state carries no meaning here (it's a log, not a work item), so every run leaves the state exactly as found and only ever appends. When the routine reports a **current state** rather than a stream of discrete changes (a branch/PR report, a status roll-up), keep that state in the issue **body**, rewritten each run so the newest snapshot is at the top, and use the dated comments as the per-run trail — the reader sees today's picture first, not the oldest one. (Worked examples: `docs/claude/auto-lessons.md` #365, `docs/claude/auto-fallback-coverage.md` #366, `docs/claude/auto-branch-report.md` #399.) **Read that log before authoring anything the routine may have attempted before** — each run re-derives its candidates independently from the same sources, so runs converge on the same item and re-hit the same rejection; make reading the log a precondition of authoring, not a formatting step at the end. **Read the open PRs touching the same paths too, for the same reason**: where the routine's output is review-gated, a finished run's work sits unmerged and the next run — reading only the default branch — cannot see it, so it redoes the work and throws the earlier PR's copy away. An open PR is work already done; when one already answers the question, say so on it and get it reviewed rather than answering it twice.

A routine whose output lands **in the repo** already has a record: the commit, the PR and the file it changed, which diff, carry history, and sit where a reader is already looking, none of which an in-place-rewritten issue body does. Where a tracker does earn its place, title it exactly `Claudinite tracker: <Name>`. Find it by that **exact title string, never a fuzzy or partial match** and never a bare number (a number can dangle, and a partial match risks landing on the wrong issue). Log every run that produces a change there — as a **dated comment**, not a sub-issue — so the routine's output accumulates in one reviewable feed, making it easy to audit what it did over time and to tell when the routine itself needs tuning. One issue per routine, not a shared parent. **Create it already closed** if it doesn't exist yet — that is **two calls**, because issue creation always lands the issue open and a `state: closed` argument on the create call is silently ignored: create it, then close it with a follow-up update. And **never open, close, or reopen it again afterward** — its state carries no meaning here (it's a log, not a work item), so every run leaves the state exactly as found and only ever appends. When the routine reports a **current state** rather than a stream of discrete changes (a branch/PR report, a status roll-up), keep that state in the issue **body**, rewritten each run so the newest snapshot is at the top, and use the dated comments as the per-run trail — the reader sees today's picture first, not the oldest one. (Worked examples: `docs/claude/auto-lessons.md` #365, `docs/claude/auto-fallback-coverage.md` #366, `docs/claude/auto-branch-report.md` #399.) **Read that log before authoring anything the routine may have attempted before** — each run re-derives its candidates independently from the same sources, so runs converge on the same item and re-hit the same rejection; make reading the log a precondition of authoring, not a formatting step at the end. **Read the open PRs touching the same paths too, for the same reason**: where the routine's output is review-gated, a finished run's work sits unmerged and the next run — reading only the default branch — cannot see it, so it redoes the work and throws the earlier PR's copy away. An open PR is work already done; when one already answers the question, say so on it and get it reviewed rather than answering it twice.

input.body:
Closes #1258

Eleven tasks kept a standing tracker issue. Eight of them were logging what automatic work did to a **local pack** — a record that belongs in the pack, in git, beside the change it describes.

## The record that replaces them

Each local pack now carries a `VERSIONS.md`, seeded empty by `seedRepoLocalPack` at adoption. A canon pack's `VERSIONS.md` is one row per version bump; a local pack is neither versioned nor distributed, so its rows are the only granularity it has — one per change automatic work made to it. Written in the same commit as the change, so it diffs beside what it records and travels with the pack.

A run that changed nothing writes no row. The file logs what happened to the pack, never that a run happened.

## Per task

| Task | Was | Now |
|---|---|---|
| `growth-extract` | `Claudinite tracker: Growth Extract` | a `VERSIONS.md` row per rule added or converted |
| `growth-discover-packs` | `Claudinite tracker: Discover Local Packs` | seeds the new pack's `VERSIONS.md`; everything else goes in the PR body the reviewer is already reading |
| `prose-to-checks-sweep` | `Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks` | a row per conversion, naming the check id |
| `rule-revalidation` | `Claudinite tracker: Rule Revalidation` | a row per rule corrected or deleted; verdicts in the PR body |
| `growth-dedup` | `Claudinite tracker: Growth Dedup` | brief → a comment on the run's own work item; a row per prune |
| `wiki-growth` | `Claudinite tracker: Product Wiki Growth` | nothing — the wiki's git history is the record; a blocked pass converges through the run's outcome |
| `jwt-advisory-watch` | `Claudinite tracker: JWT advisory watch` | a **real, open issue** only for an advisory affecting a resolved version |
| `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `ci-performance` | keep | keep — each holds a current picture nothing else does |
| `tidy-branches` | keep | untouched; #1240 removes the task |

## Three things worth a reviewer's attention

**`rule-revalidation` loses its slicing along with the tracker.** `task.md:34` picked the ten claims longest since their last recorded probe *per the tracker's log* — the tracker was state, not a record. Probing every environment-fact claim each run leaves nothing to remember. That set is far smaller than the corpus: judgment prose is already out of scope.

**`growth-dedup`'s tracker was neither log nor state** — it was the carrier for a brief that can reach GitHub's 64KB body cap, because no code→agent data channel exists (`worker.mjs:16`). Code-work already receives `CLAUDINITE_ITEM`, so the brief becomes a comment on the run's own work item: per-run, which is what the brief already was, and it dies with the item instead of outliving it by a week holding a stale window.

**`jwt-advisory-watch` dedups on the GHSA against the library, never on its own title.** Each run phrases its own title from that run's hit set, so a title match would file a duplicate the moment the set changed.

## Two engine fixes that come with it

- `findTracker` re-closes a tracker it finds **open**. `createTracker` has closed on create since #951, but nothing ever repaired one made before that — which is why #904 has sat open since 2026-08-16. The repair rides the lookup because every task's own run performs one; it is fail-soft, since an unclosable tracker is untidy, never a reason to fail the run about to write its record.
- `[claudinite] CI performance` joins the hidden-titles filter in `engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs`. It is off-convention, so `tidy-issues` was seeing it as ordinary project work.

## Verification

Full suite green (2638 pass / 0 fail), `check_the_work` and `check_the_world` both 0 blocking with no new advisories. Each behaviour change was seen failing first: the open-tracker repair, the seeded `VERSIONS.md`, and the signals filter.

Not verified here, and only observable once these land in a member's mount: that a real `growth-*` run actually writes its `VERSIONS.md` row, and that a real `jwt-advisory-watch` run files an issue rather than a tracker. Both need a production verification once merged.

---

[#1262](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1262) is open against [#1258](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1258).

```
Folders touched

engine/scheduler/          findTracker re-closes a tracker it finds open (fail-soft);
                           seedRepoLocalPack writes a VERSIONS.md beside RULES.md;
                           the issues signal now hides "[claudinite] CI performance".

packs/claudinite-growth/   Four task docs drop their tracker sections for VERSIONS.md rows;
                           rule-revalidation loses its slicing; growth-dedup's worker posts
                           the window brief to CLAUDINITE_ITEM instead of a tracker, and
                           TRACKER_TITLE is gone. New README section owns the convention,
                           new RULES.md rule points every task at it, and unattended-agents
                           now says a tracker is only for a current picture nothing else holds.

packs/jwt/                 jwt-advisory-watch stops keeping a monthly "all clean" body and
                           files a real open issue per advisory hit, deduped on the GHSA.

packs/product-wiki/        wiki-growth keeps no record beyond the wiki's git history.

.claudinite/local/packs/   VERSIONS.md created for this repo's two local packs.
```

Two things I did not do, deliberately:

- **`tidy-branches` is untouched** — [#1240](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1240) removes the task, and its tracker goes with it.
- **[#904](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/904) is still open.** The engine now re-closes it, but that happens on `ci-performance`'s next weekly run — which is the point of the fix. Closing it by hand here would prove nothing about whether the repair works.

Your instruction that open trackers should be closed by daily `tidy-issues` I've implemented one rung earlier instead: `tidy-issues` only runs when a real issue was touched, so an open tracker could sit for days waiting on unrelated activity, and it would need a second read outside the very filter that hides trackers from it. Putting the repair in the lookup every task already performs closes it on the owning task's own next run, with no change to the signal. Say the word if you'd rather have it in `tidy-issues` as well.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#1262](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1262) awaiting your review. Two claims can only be proven once merged and converged — that a real growth run writes its `VERSIONS.md` row, and that `jwt-advisory-watch` files an issue rather than a tracker — so I'll file the production verification after the merge, not before.

content.content:
---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---

# Merge to main

If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.

1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
6. Capture the conversation:
   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
7. Run the basics pack's
   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.

Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot-authored
  # PR flow (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

commit deaf7d34dc2a294bc9643e5f0f905bf0fefae873
Author: missingbulb <73882448+missingbulb@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Sun Aug 23 03:50:46 2026 +0300

    Pack manifests by convention: the tree declares the pack (#1248)
    
    * Derive a pack's id, prose, badge and skills from its directory
    
    Four manifest fields had exactly one correct value in every pack ever written —
    the one the pack's own directory already gave. The loader now reads them off the
    tree (engine/pack_loader/pack-conventions.mjs) before the spec judges the result,
    and a pack.mjs declaration overrides that only where a pack genuinely differs.
    
    Every canon pack and the local-pack seed template drop the four declarations;
    the mount now honours a manifest's skills list rather than re-deriving it, so
    withholding a skill is a real override.
    
    Delivery: a manifest with no `id` is dropped outright by a pre-convention engine,
    which fails the mount self-test and stops that member converging at all — so
    every pack's minEngineVersion rises to this engine release, and the pack update
    flow's minEngineVersion terminal holds the ordering.
    
    Refs #1246
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
    Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01HJVyZWYaTPZG5it3YJLwb5
    
    * Record engine release 60822.1, with the fixture that proves it consumer-safe
    
    The canary converged against this branch and passed its own self-test on a canon
    whose packs declare no `id` — which is what qualifies the release the packs are
    gated behind.
    
    The rehearsal gains a `convention-local` shape: a consumer-authored manifest that
    declares none of the four, beside the shapes that still declare them. The
    convention is additive, so both must converge green.
    
    Refs #1246
    
    Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.

{"total_count":1,"workflow_runs":[{"id":32609491502,"name":"CI","display_title":"Retire the growth, wiki and jwt standing trackers for the pack's VERSIONS.md","workflow_id":317526095,"run_number":1234,"run_attempt":1,"event":"pull_request","status":"in_progress","head_branch":"claude/tracker-issue-tasks-review-skxhu1","head_sha":"32ff4bf97f37144a55c6cb97ed709b0d21f92e1d","head_commit":{"message":"Retire the growth, wiki and jwt standing trackers for the pack's VERSIONS.md

Eight of eleven tasks kept a standing tracker issue that was really a log of
what automatic work did to a local pack — a record that belongs in the pack, in
git, beside the change it describes.

Each local pack now carries VERSIONS.md, seeded empty at adoption: one row per
prose rule added or removed, check created, or rule corrected against a probe.
growth-extract, growth-discover-packs, prose-to-checks-sweep, rule-revalidation
and growth-dedup write rows there instead of comments on an issue. wiki-growth
keeps no record beyond the wiki's own git history. jwt-advisory-watch stops
rewriting a monthly "all clean" body and instead files a real, open issue only
when an advisory affects a resolved version, deduped on the GHSA against the
library rather than on its own title.

rule-revalidation loses its slicing with its tracker: the log was state, not a
record — it named the claims a previous run had probed. Taking every
environment-fact claim each run leaves nothing to remember.

growth-dedup's tracker was neither, it was the carrier for a 64KB window brief,
because no code->agent data channel exists. Code-work already receives
CLAUDINITE_ITEM, so the brief becomes a comment on the run's own work item:
per-run, which is what the brief already was, and it dies with the item.

tidy-issues, tidy-prs and ci-performance keep theirs — each holds a current
picture nothing else does. Two engine fixes come with that: findTracker now
re-closes a tracker it finds open, since createTracker has closed on create
only since #951 and nothing ever repaired one made before it (#904, open since
2026-08-16); and ci-performance's off-convention title joins the filter that
hides trackers from the issues signal, where tidy-issues was seeing it as
ordinary project work.

Closes #1258
